title: Implied probability
blurb: Why 62¢ means 62%, and why it's not quite that simple.
body: A YES contract pays $1 if the event happens and $0 if it doesn't. Pay 62¢ for it and you are saying the event is at least 62% likely, because that's where the bet breaks even.

So the price is a probability, but it is a *market's* probability: it bundles what traders believe with how badly they want to be in or out, how much cash is on the book, and the fees they'll pay. A 62¢ price with a 4¢ spread means YES is somewhere between 60% and 64%, plus or minus the crowd's mood.

For mutually exclusive outcomes the YES prices should sum to about 100%. When they sum to 110%, someone is overpaying; when they sum to 70%, either the list of outcomes is incomplete or the field is cheap.
example: Five Fed-decision brackets priced 83¢ + 15¢ + 1¢ + 0.5¢ + 0.3¢ sum to 99.8%. That is a consistent book.

title: Spread and vig
blurb: The gap you pay to trade, and who collects it.
body: The spread is the distance between the best bid and the best ask. Buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and you lose the spread instantly. On a 14¢/16¢ market that round trip costs 2¢, about 13% of your stake.
Vig (short for vigorish) is the house's cut. Venues charge it as a fee on winnings or on each trade, and a wide spread is a hidden vig paid to whoever is quoting both sides.
Every edge you think you have must first beat spread plus fees. That is why the Scanner only flags a cross-venue gap when it is bigger than both venues' spreads plus an estimate of fees.
example: Kalshi 15¢ vs Polymarket 15.8¢ looks like a gap of 0.8¢. Spreads and fees cost about 5¢. No edge.

title: Liquidity
blurb: Why a thin book can move 10 points on one order.
body: Liquidity is how much you can trade without moving the price. A book with $50,000 resting at every cent barely notices a $5,000 order; a book with $200 resting moves ten points on the same order.

Thin markets produce dramatic charts that mean very little. The anomaly score looks at volume relative to a market's own history for exactly this reason: a 20× volume hour in a thin market is still a tiny amount of money.
The Swarm Simulator models this with an LMSR market maker whose liquidity parameter sets how far each dollar pushes the price.
example: A $2,000 YES order at 1,000 contracts of depth moves the price three points; the same order at 20 contracts of depth moves it to the moon and back by lunch.

title: Wash trading
blurb: Volume that looks like interest but is one hand washing the other.
body: Wash trading is trading with yourself (or a partner) to print volume. The price barely moves, but the market looks hot, climbs leaderboards, and attracts real money that provides exit liquidity.
The tell is volume without price discovery: big bars, flat price, and a handful of wallets on both sides of every trade. Real interest moves the price; fake interest just moves the volume counter.
Prediction markets have been accused of exactly this around airdrop farming and incentive programs, where volume itself was the reward.
example: Six hours of $40,000 volume on a contract that never left 51–53¢ is a chart to be suspicious of, not excited by.

title: Anomaly patterns
blurb: The shapes a price makes before news it shouldn't know yet.
body: The pattern enforcement actions describe is simple: a contract at 2¢ for weeks, a burst of concentrated buying from a few wallets, a jump to 30, 60, 90¢, and then the headline that explains it arrives hours later.

No single feature proves anything. Volume spikes happen, prices gap, and new wallets show up every day. The anomaly score combines four of these signals and tells you how unusual the hour was compared with the market's own history. It says *look here*, never *that person did it*.
Timing is the strongest clue. A move that follows the headline is a market doing its job. A move that precedes the headline by hours is a question worth asking.
In April 2026 the CFTC brought its first civil insider trading case over event contracts. The receipts in that case were price charts and wallet histories like the ones in this terminal.
example: Scenario 2 in the Scanner: a Nobel Peace Prize contract at under 1¢ runs to 68¢ ten hours before the announcement, with most buying from a handful of wallets.

title: Cross-venue arbitrage
blurb: Same event, two prices, one edge. Minus fees.
body: When two venues list the same event, their prices should match. When they don't, buy the cheap one and sell the expensive one and you lock in the difference, as long as the contracts really resolve the same way.

The catch is in the rules. 'Above 4.00%' on one venue can equal the sum of two brackets on the other, or differ by a date or a data source. The Scanner proposes pairs by title and then compares resolution text before it trusts a gap.

Also, fees and spreads on both legs come out of the gap, capital is tied up until resolution, and you need an account on both venues. Most 'arbitrage' on a screen is smaller than the friction to capture it.
example: A 3.7¢ gap on a 2028 nominee between venues shrinks to about 1.5¢ after both spreads and fees, and takes two years to pay out.
